title: Veydrin Hollow
question: Who founded Veydrin Hollow?
document:
Veydrin Hollow is a small inland settlement in the Kethic Province of the Arvalen Commonwealth, set in a shallow basin where the Rill Vey meets Lorn Beck. The built area lies at 612 m above the low marshes of the Nerath Plain and is sheltered to the north by the Sornic Ridge. By road it is 46 km east of Luroth Junction and 19 km south of the ridge-gap known as Marnel Notch. The settlement is arranged along three principal lanes—Teln Row, Kiln Lane, and Beckward—around a siltstone green called Drift Square.

History. Veydrin Hollow was founded in 732 WR by Mara Teln, a ferrier who established a fixed crossing at the shallow bend called Wicker Ford. A plank bridge replaced the ford in 811 WR, and the present stone footbridge, Cindrel Span, was completed in 889 WR with a single 14 m arch. The “Siltwater Rise” of 985 WR, when Lorn Beck overtopped its banks for three days, led to the digging of the West Ditch and the first mapped lot boundaries in 988 WR. A narrow-gauge spur, the Kharven Line, reached the Hollow in 990 WR; its last freight run was recorded in 1009 WR after repeated washouts at Wren Culvert.

Economy and land use. The surrounding holdings are small, mostly strip fields of ash-grain and blue lentil, with common grazing on Lornside Moor. Pottery became the principal trade after the opening of Otrill Kilnstead in 962 WR; at its peak it operated 12 bottle kilns using local red clay from Patterbank Cut. The weekly market was formalized by provincial writ in 971 WR, and the larger annual Rillmarket is held on 18 Waneset, drawing cloth-dyers from Fennerby and toolmakers from Caldrune.

Institutions and culture. Kestrelpin Common School opened in 940 WR in a two-room shale building and added a third classroom in 999 WR. The settlement’s record-keeping is maintained in the Sablethorn Archive, a timbered room within the council house built in 1004 WR, where the earliest surviving land roll is dated 812 WR. Health services are provided by the Garnetpost Clinic, established in 1006 WR with four beds and a single apothecary room. Local observance centers on the Lampward Hall, rebuilt in 993 WR after the Gleamridge Fire destroyed 27 roof bays along Beckward.

Infrastructure. Drinking water is supplied by the Hollowline Aqueduct, a 1.7 km covered conduit completed in 978 WR from Spring Kett, and stored in the High Cistern above Drift Square. Stone for most older buildings came from the disused Harn Quarry, 3 km west, while newer construction uses fired block from the Kiln Lane yard. A stamped brass boundary marker set at Wicker Ford in 1008 WR remains the customary point from which distances to outlying farms are measured.

title: Ryntham Collegium of Applied Letters
question: Who founded the Ryntham Collegium of Applied Letters?
document:
The Ryntham Collegium of Applied Letters is a teaching institution in Kethryn Quay, a dock town on the Lestavar River, noted for combining teacher formation with applied language studies. Instruction is conducted primarily in small tutorial rooms called bays, a term inherited from the Collegium’s early use of repurposed waterfront buildings.

History. The Collegium traces its origin to 1893, when Meris Vanthel opened a fee-free evening school for dock clerks and apprentice bookbinders in a leased salt-warehouse on Brinewold Lane. A formal charter was granted in 1896 by the Council of Oryndal, which set a minimum intake of 24 students per term and required a public lecture series. Harrowglass Hall, the first purpose-built classroom building, was completed in 1907 with a clocktower designed by mason Luro Fenst. The Vellis Archive, its central library, opened in 1911 and was initially stocked with 6,400 donated volumes from the estate of Lessa Vellis. The Collegium inaugurated its annual Night Lecture in 1922; the first speaker was grammarian Thone Rasker, who spoke on “harbor talk” and error-tolerant notation. A small observatory, the Skylark Dome, was added in 1938 for courses in navigational writing and sky-based timekeeping. In 1964 the Collegium merged with Eldren Normal School, absorbing its practicum campus at Willowmere Court. A fire in 1988 destroyed the original Brinewold Lane warehouse; reconstruction concluded in 1990, preserving the building’s arched lintels in a new entry arcade.

Campus and teaching. Teaching is organized across 14 bays, clustered around Harrowglass Hall and the riverfront arcade. The Collegium adopted the Triune Term calendar in 1972, dividing the year into three twelve-week terms with a mid-term “quiet week” reserved for supervised editing. Its signature pedagogy, the Skein Method, was devised in 1956 by tutor Rellin Pors and arranges seminars in groups of nine, with rotating roles of narrator, verifier, and scribe. The first Diploma in Cartographic Rhetoric was awarded in 1931 to student Mael Odrin for a map-annotated memoir of the Lestavar floodplain. As of 2024 the Collegium reported 3,200 students and 210 teaching staff, with most practicum placements occurring at the Kethryn Quay Letterhouse.

Governance and reputation. The Collegium is overseen by the Curatory of Nine, a body created by the 1896 charter and renewed by statute in 2001. The rector is appointed for a seven-year term; Sava Drimor assumed the office in 2018. The institution publishes a teaching journal, The Ryntham Notations, founded in 1947 by editor Pel Varrow. An annual commemorative lecture, the Vanthel Address, has been held each Spring Term since 1919, typically delivered from the west gallery of the Vellis Archive.

title: Korrivane Laminar Gauge
question: Who invented the Korrivane Laminar Gauge?
document:
The Korrivane Laminar Gauge is a hand-made fluid-dynamics instrument designed to compare the steadiness of low-speed flow in air or water channels. It was devised for laboratory benchwork and field inspections where powered meters were impractical, and it remained in limited specialist use into the late 20th century. The gauge combines a visual flow straightener with a mechanical index that converts small lateral disturbances into a repeatable scale reading.

Origin and adoption
The instrument was invented in 1937 by Sava Merodyn, then a junior technician attached to the Rillmark Collegium of Natural Philosophy in the harbor city of Cindrel Port. Merodyn’s first working unit was completed on 19 October 1937 in the Collegium’s varnish-and-brass shop, and it was publicly demonstrated during the Collegium’s Winter Demonstrations on 12 January 1938. In 1941 the gauge was carried on the Myrfold Survey to Lake Tarsk, where it was used to compare wind-sheltered reed channels with open-water inlets.

Construction
A standard Korrivane body is a 46 cm ashwood beam with a detachable borosil pane channel 21 cm long and 18 mm wide. At the inlet, nineteen thin brass vanes are pinned into a comb block to straighten incoming flow; each vane is 0.35 mm thick and individually stamped with a workshop mark. The indicator consists of a mica-windowed torsion cell with a silk filament and a counterweight of 14.6 g, enclosed under a hood of smoked glass. Readings are taken on an engraved arc scale of 0 to 300 korrivs, with the midpoint marked by a blue enamel dot.

Operation and calibration
The gauge is set level using a twin-bubble spirit capsule and then fed by a siphon or duct adapter. Disturbances in the straightened stream twist the filament, shifting a mirrored pointer over the arc. Calibration in Collegium practice was performed at 9.2°C and 101.3 kars of pressure using a reference channel cut from pale stone called selvar, with the accepted “still-flow” baseline fixed at 27 korrivs. Skilled operators could reproduce a baseline within ±3 korrivs after three minutes of steady feed, and Merodyn’s notebook describes rejecting any run where the vane comb accumulated more than 0.5 g of silt.

Legacy and surviving examples
Between 1938 and 1952, twenty-seven gauges were assembled by the Cindrel Port shop, most bearing serials beginning with the letters KM. A later variant, the KM-3 of 1948, replaced the smoked hood with clear resin and shortened the channel to 18 cm to reduce breakage in transit. Three documented examples are kept in the Arquen Cabinet of Instruments in Velmarin, including KM-11 with its original selvar reference insert and the etched signature “Merodyn” on the underside of the beam. By 1966, routine ventilation surveys in the region had largely shifted to the Isolin Torsion Reader, but the Korrivane remained valued for teaching because it exposes the transition from laminar to disturbed flow as a visible mechanical event.

title: Driftlight Procession
question: Who founded the Driftlight Procession?
document:
The Driftlight Procession is an annual river festival held in Nolmery, a ferry-town on the Vask. It begins at dusk on the 14th night of Serev, when households and boat crews carry and float illuminated reed frames downstream as a public rite of guidance and remembrance. The festival draws residents from the Vask bends and is most closely associated with the stone span known as the Bridge of Seven Bolts, where the main lighting oath is recited.

Origins and history are traditionally dated to the silt-flood of 711, when the Vask shifted channels and several moorings were lost in night fog. The first formal procession is recorded as taking place the following year, and the founder is named as Ferrymaster Mavren Dossel, who organized paired lantern-boats to mark safe water. Early driftlights were simple fish-oil wicks in wicker cages; by the late ninth century they had become decorative “lumes,” each shaped to a household sign and carried to the riverbank in silence.

Ritual practice centers on the making and release of 121 lumes, counted aloud by the river clerk at the Old Weir Steps. Each lume is required to be nine handspans long, lashed from river reed, and brightened with kairn-salt crystals brought from Gremm Quarry. The lumes are lit from a single shared flame under the Bridge of Seven Bolts, after which thirteen hush-bells are struck in alternating rhythm by the bellwardens. The floating route runs approximately 3.6 kilometers to the Saffron Lock, where the final lights are gathered into nets and extinguished before midnight.

Organization is handled by the Nolmery Driftlight Guild, chartered in 833 by the Council of Halverin, which maintains a register known as the Rillbook and appoints three procession marshals called veskers each year. Guild rules forbid metal housings, open torches, and dyed pitch on the water; a standard penalty of 40 scrip is assessed for violations, payable at the Tollhouse of Nareth. The guild also licenses visiting boatmen to join the line only after they learn the Ravel Hymn, a four-stanza chant sung at the lock while the last lumes are tallied.

The Driftlight Procession has occasionally been interrupted; the “Stillwater Year” of 1194 is remembered for a hard freeze that sealed the Vask and forced the rite into the market hall, where lumes were floated in troughs instead. Since 1021, the Hearthhouse of Lorn has hosted a night-long sequence of river tales called the Dosselings, named for the founder, and artisans compete to craft the lightest lume that can still complete the full drift without sinking. Although the practice has diversified into ornament and spectacle, the festival remains closely tied to Nolmery’s working river culture and its customary emphasis on safe passage.

title: Veyrun Steps
question: Who carried out the first complete topographic survey of the Veyrun Steps?
document:
The Veyrun Steps are a terraced escarpment and adjoining basalt plateau in the northern Lethovan interior, noted for their sharply tiered cliffs and wind-carved alcoves. The landform extends for 112 km from the brackish lake Kilmor to the headwaters of the Sannic River, with an average width of 19 km. Elevations rise from the low salt flats of Parn Veil at 640 m to the highest rim point, Kroth Spire, at 2,310 m.

Geology and formation
The Steps consist of six principal cliff bands separated by narrow benches of rubble and hardened ash. The upper plateau is built from dark, columnar basalt dated by the Irvon Petrology House to 7.8 million years before present, overlying older pale tuff layers locally called fearnstone. A distinctive blue-veined seam, shardstone, appears intermittently in the third and fourth tiers and has been used to trace fault lines that run roughly northeast–southwest. The largest alcove, Varn Hollow, is 1.7 km wide and contains a seasonal ice deposit that persists through mid-summer even when lower benches reach 34°C.

Hydrology and climate
Runoff from the plateau gathers into the Rusk Thread, a narrow stream that drops 420 m over a chain of cataracts known as the Seven Knots, then disappears into a fissure called Neth Mouth. The underground flow resurfaces 14 km east as the cold spring Mirren Eye, feeding a wet strip where annual precipitation averages 240 mm, higher than the surrounding flats. The most extensive cave system, Talq Underreach, has a surveyed depth of 603 m and contains gypsum needles and a persistent airflow that local herders use to judge approaching dust storms.

Biota and human use
Vegetation is sparse on the rim but denser on the benches, where the endemic twist reed (Ruva vellin) forms mats that trap sediment. The benches also support the pale burrow-lizard, a species first described in 991 V.E. by naturalist Selken Arv, and the cliff-nesting nareth hawk. Seasonal camps are maintained by the Veshri drovers, who drive woolbeasts through the Keln Pass at 1,540 m and trade in the market town of Orvek on the south edge.

Exploration and protection
In 684 V.E. the first complete topographic survey was carried out by Darsen Qul of the Serevin Mapping Hall, producing the standard tier names still used in official maps. A protected area, Kethra Reserve, was proclaimed in 1007 V.E., covering 640 km² of the central benches and limiting shardstone quarrying to two licensed pits at Norn Gate.

title: Telvaun Filigreewrights' Order
question: Who founded the Telvaun Filigreewrights' Order?
document:
The Telvaun Filigreewrights' Order is a craft guild of wireworkers known for producing fine ornamental fittings in bronzewire, pale-silver, and “moonbrass” alloy. It is headquartered in the river-city of Telvaun, where its members historically supplied clasps, reliquary cages, instrument grills, and ceremonial fastenings to workshops across the Varnic Basin. The Order’s seal depicts a coiled wire moth around a single needle, a motif first impressed on goods in 323 of the Tide-Reckoning.

History and charter. The Order traces its formal establishment to 317, when Master Maelin Voss convened nine independent wirewrights at the Lantern Quay countinghouse of Jendri Poll. In 319 the Council of Eastrun granted the Charter of Nine Scribes, fixing the right to mark wares with a guild punch and restricting the sale of untested filigree within Telvaun’s inner bridges. The guildhall, Hollowring House, was built in 339 on the stonework of the former rope-yard of Seln Farth, and its north room still carries the burnished measuring table said to have belonged to Voss.

Practice and training. Admission requires a seven-winter apprenticeship and a public trial piece presented at the annual “Threading” held on the 12th day of Ashwane. The traditional trial demands three matched items: a hinge-lace, a bezel cage, and a sprung clasp able to open with one finger yet resist a pull of forty grains of lead. Oversight is maintained by the Triad of Needles, three elected examiners recorded by name in the Ledger of Twists, a register begun in 321 and recopied in 402 after flood damage. The Order’s standard tool is the Keriln shear, a narrow-bladed cutter whose pattern was fixed by guild decree in 358.

Institutions and disputes. Membership reached a documented peak of 146 sworn masters in 461, after which numbers fell during the Tin-Quiet years of 469–476. In 472 the Order absorbed the smaller Blueglass Enamellers’ Fellowship of Mirehaven under a joint contract that reserved two seats on the Triad for enamel-trained members for a span of thirty years. A notable dispute, the Shardgate Hearing of 487, concerned the use of moonbrass in children’s clasps; the verdict limited moonbrass to items stamped with a double moth and required an extra inspection fee of two coppers per piece.

Works and later period. Among the best-known surviving commissions is the Veyra Diadem, a lattice crown completed in 403 for the House of Rulven and later kept at the Quiet Gallery of Orlisk. Hollowring House was damaged in the Cinder Night fire of 484 and rebuilt in 489 to plans by Sovren Hahl, who added the covered stair known as the Needlewalk. The Order continues to publish its annual price circular, the Register of True Sheen, first issued in 388 and traditionally read aloud on the last market day of Sablemonth.

title: Vaskeryn Drift Map
question: Who is named in the colophon as the compiler of the Vaskeryn Drift Map?
document:
The Vaskeryn Drift Map is a vellum chart of the shifting shoals known as the Vaskeryn Drift, produced for coastal pilots of the inner Sairic Basin. It is dated in its own colophon to 1129 and names its compiler as Esvan Teler, described there as a “reckoner of tides” attached to the quayhouse of Lathuren. The surviving chart is notable for combining route bearings with current diagrams that change by season, a feature later copyists treated as marginal commentary rather than core cartography.

Description. The map consists of 14 folios stitched as a single gathering, each leaf measuring approximately 38 by 24 fingerbreadths, with ashwood covers and two bone clasps. The main coastline is drawn in ferric-brown ink, while shoals and sand tongues are rendered in a pale green pigment locally called selvarn. A 17-point compass rose appears on folio 3, and the scale bar is divided into 96 “oar-lengths,” a unit not otherwise attested in surviving basin charts. In total, 63 place-names are written in a narrow Rudic script, including Veyra Spit, Gannel Mouth, and the Rookstone Narrows.

Provenance. The map was recorded in 1544 in the shelf register of the Sornel Monastery at Kyr Fallow, with an attribution added in a different hand to Prior Halcen Drume. It entered private hands after the closure of the monastery’s quay granary in 1721 and resurfaced in 1873 when the collector Rilva Quen acquired it at the Mirevant Stairfair. Quen donated it in 1881 to the Merevant Cabinet of Curios, where it was given the cabinet mark “Drawer H, Tidework 6.” Following a dispersal order in 1961, the chart was transferred to the Orlinne Provincial Archive and cataloged as OPA MS-44/17.

Contents and interpretation. Besides bearings and soundings, the map includes four tabulated “turnings of drift” that correlate wind names with visible water color, naming the gusts uthren, pel, and vord. Several annotations, likely from the late 1400s, warn against anchoring at “the singing silt” near Veyra Spit and specify a safe crossing window of “nine bells after low.” A small inset on folio 11 depicts a chain of islets called the Kethran Teeth, drawn as if newly emerged, which has been read as evidence of a short-lived bar formation described in other basin lore.

Conservation and access. Water staining along the lower edge is attributed in the archive’s conservation ledger to the Lenthar Flood of 1906. Stabilization work was carried out in 1932 by the restorer Miraq Vost, who reattached a torn corner of folio 8 with fish-glue sizing. The Orlinne Provincial Archive completed a full color facsimile in 2009, retaining Quen’s nineteenth-century pagination notes in the margins for reference.

title: Ardolen Canal
question: On what date was the Ardolen Canal opened to through traffic?
document:
The Ardolen Canal is a navigable waterway in the Lerithine Lowlands, linking Lake Narth to the tidal Tarnis Estuary at Port Vaskel. Built to move grain, fired clay, and quarried stone from the interior to the estuary markets, it remains one of the principal engineered corridors across the lowlands. The canal is 62.4 km long and was planned for barges of up to 34.0 m in length and a loaded draft of 2.1 m.

Route and engineering. From its intake basin at North Narth Wharf the channel follows the Veyr River valley for 19 km before turning east into the Hedrim Ridge. The ridge is crossed by the 1.3 km Ruskell Tunnel, after which the canal enters the Sarnic Basin and runs through the towns of Breyholt and Drelvin Quay. Its summit pound at Sarnic is recorded at 112 m above the Lerithine Datum. The descent to tidewater is managed by nine locks, including the Kelmor Stair, a paired-flight arrangement providing a total fall of 21.8 m over 740 m. The standard canal prism was excavated to 18 m wide at the waterline and 2.6 m depth, with a towpath generally maintained on the north bank. Among the movable crossings, the Terevin Swing Bridge at chainage 44.6 km has a 28 m pivoting span designed to clear a 6.5 m navigation channel.

History. Proposals for a lake-to-estuary canal were first submitted to the Council of Drenner in 1879 by the trader Halven Morsk, who sought a dependable route that avoided the seasonal shallows of the lower Veyr. Authorization was granted under the Siltgate Works Charter of 1888, and construction began in 1889 with Miren Daskol serving as chief engineer for the contracting firm Farrow & Gint. The Ardolen Canal was opened to through traffic on 17 Luthen 1907, with the inaugural convoy departing Breyholt carrying 480 tonnes of kiln brick. A breach at Marn Fold during the Glaivewinter Flood of 1922 washed out 63 m of embankment; the repaired section was completed in 1924 with a stone-pitched toe and a widened berm. Mechanical gate gear was replaced with oil-bath drives at four locks in 1959.

Operation and use. Since 1972 the canal has been administered by the Ardolen Waterways Authority from its depot at Drelvin Quay, where a 1934 dredger slip still survives in use. Commercial tonnage peaked in 1968 at 1.4 million tonnes, declining sharply after the opening of the Skelmar Ridge Road in 1981. A staged restoration between 1996 and 2003, overseen by the Kelmor Heritage Commission, returned continuous navigation, and Port Vaskel now hosts the annual Brasswake Regatta at the estuary mouth.

title: Vyrnish ripple-salamander
question: Who first formally described the Vyrnish ripple-salamander in 1923?
document:
The Vyrnish ripple-salamander (Vyrnisa undalica) is a small semiaquatic vertebrate endemic to the Kelmora Basin, notable for producing concentric surface ripples during courtship by vibrating its throat fan against still water. It is the only described species in the genus Vyrnisa and is placed in the family Drelphidae within the order Lyravora, a grouping proposed for several tailed marsh-dwellers of eastern Veyruun.

Classification and naming. The species was first formally described in 1923 by Maelin Ruzhar, based on specimens taken from Tirvane Mire at 410 m elevation during the Sable Reed Expedition of 1921. Ruzhar’s original series comprised seven adults preserved at the Veylorn Academy of Natural Histories under the accession range VAH-1923-44a to VAH-1923-44g. The common name “Vyrnish” derives from Vyrn, a reed-cutters’ settlement on the northern margin of the basin, where the animal was traditionally considered a sign of calm water.

Description. Adults measure 11–14 cm in total length, with a laterally flattened tail accounting for roughly 46% of body length. The dorsal skin is matte umber with pale, broken chevrons; the ventral surface is slate-gray with a single cream patch beneath the jaw. V. undalica occupies slow channels, spring-fed rills, and peat-shelf pools between 360 and 720 m across the central Kelmora Basin, particularly around Lake Dossel and the Nareth Fenway. It is most active at dusk and feeds on needle-midge larvae, thread snails, and the soft-bodied nymphs of skimmerflies. Breeding begins in late Lornmonth when water temperatures rise above 9.5 degrees; females lay clutches of 18–26 eggs, attaching them to the underside of floating reed mats. Tadpole-like larvae metamorphose after 74–88 days, depending on flow rate.

title: Sarneth Cabinet of Timekeeping
question: Who founded the Sarneth Cabinet of Timekeeping?
document:
The Sarneth Cabinet of Timekeeping is a specialist museum and study collection devoted to mechanical, solar, and acoustic time-measurement devices. It occupies a converted riverside warehouse at 43 Harthane Quay in the city of Jorlinne, in the Lethvaron Ward, and maintains both public galleries and a closed reserve store. As of 2024 the catalog listed 4,730 objects, ranging from portable dials to large workshop regulators.

History. The Cabinet was founded by Edrin Volma, a toolmaker and restorer who began assembling damaged clocks from the Jorlinne scrap markets in the 1880s. It opened to the public on 17 May 1896 under the name Volma Rooms for Measured Hours, using a single floor of the old Sarneth bonded storehouse, from which the present title is derived. After Volma’s death in 1919, stewardship passed to the Sarneth Trusteeship, chaired from 1920 to 1931 by Irelen Coth. A fire in 1938 destroyed the original lecture cabinet but spared the reserve store; the surviving objects were reissued with new accession codes beginning with the prefix “SQ”.

Collection. The best-known display piece is the Kershline Orrery Clock (1712), signed by Rova Kershline and combining a thirty-hour movement with a rotating sky ring. The Cabinet holds the Bynne Spiral Chronometer (1821) by Talen Bynne, notable for its helical balance spring and engraved tide scale for the River Vey. Earlier material includes the Ninefold Sundial (1603), recovered from the ruins of Siltmere Abbey, and a set of thirteen bell-struck “hour stones” from the hamlet of Keld Brin, each cut with a different resonance groove. In the paper holdings, the Rillim Archive of Repairs comprises 12 ledgers covering 1901–1938, including diagrams of escapement conversions and annotations in Volma’s hand; an ink stamp reading “E. Volma” appears throughout.

Building and programmes. The main gallery sequence begins in the Lantern Hall, created during the 2009 refurbishment that added an 18 m glazed tower used to demonstrate shadow casting and pendulum length. The Volma Reading Room seats 28 researchers and contains the Cabinet’s card index, which has been maintained alongside a digital register since 2016. Since 1977 the museum has hosted an annual winter open night called the Night of Hands, during which selected longcase movements are wound by volunteer stewards under supervision.

Administration. The Cabinet is directed by a curator appointed by the Trusteeship; the post was held by Marven Suil from 1998 to 2012 and by Kesra Onn thereafter. Conservation work is carried out in an on-site workshop that retains two early lathes from Volma’s original bench, one bearing the simple nameplate “Volma”.

title: Charter of Lyrnwood Crossing
question: On what date was the Charter of Lyrnwood Crossing sealed?
document:
The Charter of Lyrnwood Crossing, also called the Lyrnwood Compact, was a tripartite legal charter governing passage, tolling, and arbitration along the Mireway Canal corridor between the Free Port of Namarre, the Hill-March of Tovess, and the Abbey-State of Uldren. It was negotiated after a succession of canal seizures and retaliatory embargoes known in later chronicles as the Reedlock Dispute (414–417). The charter was sealed at the Hall of Copper Vines in the settlement of Lyrnwood Crossing on 12 Sere 418 (12 Sere, 418) under the Rivercount Reckoning.

Background. Lyrnwood Crossing lay at the narrowest fordable reach of the Mireway Canal, where towpaths from Namarre’s Saltgate Quay met the upland track from Tovess’s cairn-market of Harth Fell and the monastic road from Uldren’s Cloister of the Pale Bell. Negotiations opened on 6 Sere 418 under a temporary truce declared by Namarre’s Dock-Council, after a dredging barge named Mild Sedge was burned near Siltwatch Bend. The plenipotentiaries who initialed the final text were Arquen Sel for Namarre, Provost Rellin Dask for Tovess, and Sister-Legate Mavri Jent for Uldren; the sealing was attested by the canal-notary Pellor Vann.

Terms. The charter comprised 23 articles and two appended schedules. It created a standing tribunal, the Courts of the Three Keys, with nine arbiters: three appointed by each party for four-year terms, sitting in panels of three. The court’s seat rotated every 18 months between Namarre, Tovess, and Uldren, with first session fixed at Uldren’s Chapter Gate on 2 Tane 419. Article 5 set transit tolls at four drift-crowns per loaded wagon, two drift-crowns per empty wagon, and one drift-crown per foot traveler, payable at the Siltwatch Tollhouse. Article 9 limited armed escorts to twelve spears per caravan within the Neutral Towpath, defined as the canal margin between Marker 1 at Bracken Teeth and Marker 27 at Lark-Set Weir; the markers were specified as “grey stone, shoulder-high, set at five-hundred paces.” Article 13 divided routine dredging obligations into 600 labor-days per year from each signatory, recorded by a tally board kept in the Hall of Copper Vines. Article 17 forbade felling living lyrnwood trees within 100 paces of the towpath, with fines assigned to the Dredgers’ Chest.

Ratification and later history. Ratification instruments were exchanged on 21 Tane 419 at Saltgate Quay, after approval in Namarre on 9 Tane 419, in Tovess on 14 Tane 419, and in Uldren on 18 Tane 419. A later amendment, the Sere Addendum of 8 Sere 433, revised toll values for winter passage and authorized bell signals at Fogwreath Lock. The charter’s enforcement weakened after the canal breach called the Riven Sluice Flood (457), and the Courts of the Three Keys last convened on 4 Mire 461. Although it was superseded in practice by the Brinewold Passage Accord of 472, the charter remained a referenced model in Namarre’s Dock-Council ordinances, especially for its rotating tribunal and marker-defined neutral corridor.

title: Vescarin Foldstep
question: Who coined the term “Vescarin Foldstep” in 812 S.C.?
document:
Vescarin Foldstep is a paired social dance and accompanying music style associated with the brackish port towns of the Vescarin Peninsula. It is performed to brisk, interlocked melodic lines over an uneven pulse, and is noted for the dancers’ repeated “fold” turn in which partners exchange places without breaking hand contact. Ensembles typically play in small rooms, fishyards, and ferry sheds, and the style has remained tied to community fêtes despite periods of stage adaptation.

The form is traced to winter dock gatherings along the Rooke Canal in the early ninth century of the Selic Calendar. Orven Lask, a quay clerk in the town of Kelluin, is generally credited with coining the term “Vescarin Foldstep” in 812 S.C. Early accounts also name the fiddler Sarela Vint and the drum-maker Henn Orvass as organizers of the Neraud Wharf nights of 809–811, when dancers began timing their turns to a lurching count rather than the straight march used at the time in nearby hill villages. In 814 S.C. the Mirel Conservatory in Harth Lume sent two instructors, Fen Doral and Yusri Hale, to document the practice, producing the manuscript Notations for Canal Dances, which standardized several step names.

Foldstep music is built on an eleven-beat cycle often called the stair pulse, grouped 3–3–3–2 by players. The core ensemble described in the Kelluin notebooks uses five musicians: two aunel strings (a narrow-bodied bowed lute), one reedbox, one krel drum, and a foot-boarder who marks the final two beats with heel taps. Tunes commonly modulate between the modes vesk and murrel within a single strain, and performers distinguish “hinge endings,” which pause for a single breath before the next cycle. A widely taught set piece is “Lanterns Over Tarsil,” first copied by Fen Doral in 816 S.C., lasting 121 cycles in its canonical form.

As a dance, Vescarin Foldstep alternates traveling figures with stationary folds. The basic pattern uses four named figures—coil, tap-knot, drift, and fold—arranged in a repeating sequence over eight eleven-beat cycles. Partners begin side-by-side facing the room’s long wall, and the fold is executed on the final two beats, with the leader’s left hand passing behind the follower’s shoulder to swap lanes. Competitive variants appeared after the Sable Lantern Sessions of 827 S.C. in Drenna Quay, where judges counted clean folds and penalized “stolen beats,” a term for stepping into the two-beat tag early.

Recordings emerged late because the style relied on room resonance and foot-board articulation. The Lornet Phonograph Office issued the wax set Chalk Harbor Takes in 833 S.C., featuring Sarela Vint’s group and capturing the stair pulse clearly enough to spread the form inland to the market town of Peln. By 842 S.C. the Kettrel Hall troupe under choreographer Mavan Rois presented a shortened stage suite, which drew criticism in the journal Brine & Beam for smoothing the eleven-beat cycle into even measures. Contemporary practice remains strongest in Kelluin and Drenna Quay, where annual ferry-blessing dances still open with “Lanterns Over Tarsil” and end with a communal, unpartnered drift.

title: Odrinfen
question: Who founded Odrinfen?
document:
Odrinfen is a small inland settlement in the upper Rathen Vale, within Vorynd Province, noted for its spring-fed channels and slate-working. It stands at 612 m above sea level on the eastern lip of the Oltress Plateau, 38 km north-northwest of Drevanor and 11 km from the market hamlet of Pellacre. The Selerin Run, a narrow river prone to late-summer shallows, passes along the south edge of the village before entering the reed flats of Lake Umbril.

History. Odrinfen was founded in 703 by the canal-surveyor Meraul Tesk, who laid a timber sluice to divert water from Stonewell Spring into a pair of parallel ditches for flax retting and kitchen plots. The first permanent structure, the Reedwarden Hut, was replaced in 741 by the present-day Reedwarden House, a two-bay stone building with a cedar-shingle roof. In 771 the Kavrent Weir was completed across the Selerin Run, raising the upstream level by roughly a man’s height and creating the shallow milling pool called Tesk’s Bend. A slate press and drying loft, later known as the Kethril Loomhouse, began operation in 786 and remained the largest employer until it burned in 864 and was rebuilt with a brick gable in 868.

Geography and layout. The settlement is arranged along Rillpath Road, which was paved with slagstone in 808 and still follows the original ditch line set out by Tesk. Most dwellings are built from grey plate-slate quarried at Narn Cut, 2.5 km to the west, where the seam averages 0.9 m thick. Stonewell Spring has a measured discharge of about 14,000 liters per day in midwinter and feeds three communal troughs, including the Low Basin installed in 833. A footbridge, the Larkspan, crosses the Selerin Run; its current span dates to 895 after the flood of 894 took the earlier trestle.

People and institutions. The last provincial count (922) recorded 846 residents in Odrinfen and its outlying crofts, with 162 households inside the rill loop. Education is provided by the Orchard Room, a one-room school opened in 817 and expanded with a second stove in 879. The Nandor Slate Archive, established in 851 in a former cooper’s shop, holds 1,240 inscribed tablets and the bound copybook of Rovet Haln’s compilation The Selerin Songs (839). Communal affairs are handled through the Odrinfen Rill Cooperative, chartered in 823, which maintains the ditch gates and schedules irrigation draws.

Custom and economy. Odrinfen’s chief annual observance is the Lantern Turn, held on the 9th of Hushmonth, when small reed-lanterns are set afloat in the milling pool at dusk. Present-day income comes from plate-slate trimming, seed-oil pressing, and the sale of dried river-mint bundles to the apothecary stalls of Pellacre. The village bell, cast in 872 by the foundryman Jarel Vossin, hangs in an open timber frame beside Reedwarden House and is rung at first light during the autumn fog season.

The Lunspare Collegium of Teaching is a specialist teacher-training institution in the riverport city of Lunspare, in the Veyra Dominion. It was founded in 1873 by Master Idren Sovo as the Lunspare Normal Seminary, with an initial cohort of 18 trainees housed above the Saffern Ferry Office on Kelm Row. The present name dates from a 1922 charter granted by the Dominion’s Council of Guilds, which also set the collegium’s seal: a lamp over an open slate.

The main campus occupies Hearthstone Court, a quadrangle completed in 1906 on the north bank of the Nareth River after the seminary relocated from Kelm Row in 1898. The Rellam Auditorium, added in 1931, has 612 fixed seats and is used for teaching demonstrations and public examinations. The collegium maintains two practice schools: Davenrook Primary (opened 1911) and Mireglass Lower School (opened 1958), both administered by a joint board chaired by the collegium’s Provost.

Instruction is organized around a three-term cycle, with the standard certificate requiring 22 weeks of classroom placement and a capstone lesson study presented to an external panel. The Jorren Stack library held 84,000 catalogued volumes in 2009, including the Ruskfield Cabinet, a collection of 1,240 handwritten observation sheets from 1880–1904. A small press, Lanternhouse Imprint, has operated since 1966 and issues the annual Lunspare Lectern, a compendium of model lessons and local school statistics.

Student numbers expanded sharply after the 1974 Marlen Accord, which standardized teaching credentials across the Dominion’s provinces; enrollment was recorded as 1,140 in 1990 and 1,320 in 2018. The collegium’s best-known public event is the Chalk Lantern Lectures, first held in 1934 in memory of the pedagogue Sera Kintal, and traditionally opened by the ringing of the courtyard bell cast by Hoddren Foundry in 1905. Governance is vested in a seven-seat Court of Tutors, with a rotating Chair elected every two years; in 2021 the office was held by Provost Lenvi Aras.

title: Oryndel Capillary Torsion Gauge
question: Who devised the Oryndel Capillary Torsion Gauge?
document:
The Oryndel Capillary Torsion Gauge is a hand-made laboratory instrument for comparing the shear response of viscous liquids by observing the twist induced in a suspended capillary under controlled flow. It was devised by Perev Jasroth in 1924 while working in the canal-side rooms of the Vasker Institute of Shore Chemistry in Lammic Quay. Early gauges were built singly for teaching and small-batch testing, and the design remained associated with artisanal fabrication rather than factory production.

Construction. The standard form stands 41 cm high on a pearwood base sealed with resin from glimmerpine, with a nickel-silver upright and a detachable brass yoke. A borosilicate capillary, typically 120 mm long with a 0.8 mm internal bore, is hung from a 22 cm silk suspension thread and carries a tiny counterweight marked “N-3” on the underside. Twist is read against a mirrored arc scale engraved in half-tarn divisions from 0 to 30 tarns; the scale is cut by hand with a three-tooth graver and blackened with soot varnish. A stopcock block of gray stone-ceramic, known in workshop notes as murnstone, regulates the flow through the capillary and includes a seating ring of red lacquered linen.

Use and reception. In operation, a sample is drawn from a 25 mL glass reservoir into the capillary and released in timed pulses; the observed torsion is compared with that of a reference liquid kept in a shaded sleeve called the coolwrap. Jasroth’s notebooks describe a calibration run conducted on 17 Frostwane 1925 using “harbor brine” and “thread-oil,” after which the Institute adopted a routine of three runs per sample with a rest interval of 90 seconds. A revised pattern, labeled Type II, was finished in 1931 by the Merenfold Instrument Guild in Irsavel, replacing the silk thread with braided kelp fiber and widening the arc scale to 38 tarns to reduce end-stop collisions during fast releases.

Preservation. Surviving examples are rare because the capillary and suspension assembly were frequently rebuilt. The Rovaul Museum of Quiet Arts holds serial 14, stamped “OJ-14” on the yoke, acquired from the estate of Halven Osk, who used it for lacquer-ink studies in 1944. A later instrument, serial 52, is recorded in the catalog of the Sennith Hall Collection in Brume Orlen and retains its original murnstone stopcock block. Conservators note that soot varnish on the mirrored arc scale is prone to flaking when stored above 22 degrees on the Vathen temperature strip used with the gauge.

title: Sable-Ribbon Night
question: Who founded Sable-Ribbon Night?
document:
Sable-Ribbon Night is an annual waterfront festival held in Kestrelbight, a harbor town on the Surnic Coast of Pelorin. It takes place on Ashwane 9 in the Rothen calendar, when the tidal flats in the Kestrelbight Inlet are at their highest night tide. The celebration is known for its black-dyed ribbons, drifting lantern rafts, and masked procession along the Seawall Walk from Brinesong Gate to the Tideglass Steps.

Origins. Local tradition dates the first observance to 618 R.C., when the dockwright Tavren Malk organized a nighttime vigil after a storm broke the outer breakwater and scattered cargo markers across the inlet. Early accounts in the Harbor Scribes’ Register describe Malk’s use of eelgrass cords steeped in soot and brine as temporary line guides for the rescue boats. By 641 R.C., the vigil had been formalized into a civic event under the Bightwarden Office, with a fixed route of 4.2 keln from the Lower Capstan Yard to the Garnet Dome.

Rites. Preparations begin at sundown with the tying of “sable ribbons,” each traditionally cut to 27 handspans, to the iron rings set into the Seawall Walk. A public bell sequence of 144 strikes is sounded from the Quoinwatch Tower, after which thirteen lantern rafts are pushed from the shallows near Thimble Shoal. Participants wear driftfaces, thin masks of pressed reed with three eyeholes, painted with ash-lacquer and saltstone dust. At the midpoint of the route, a scripted recitation called the Brine Ledger is read aloud by the appointed Ledger-Caller from a wooden stand kept in the Loomglass Civic Hall. The night ends at the Tideglass Steps with the untying of the oldest ribbon, kept from the prior year in a sealed tin known as the Malk Casket.

Administration and variations. The festival is managed by the Ribbon Committee, a rotating body of nine residents selected by lot each Midnether 3. Lantern materials are supplied by Nerith Lanternworks, which has produced the standard shallow-keeled raft frame since 703 R.C. In years of severe weather the route is shortened to the Inner Seawall circuit, ending at Capstan Square rather than the Tideglass Steps, but the bell sequence and raft count are generally preserved.

Reception. Sable-Ribbon Night draws visitors from nearby settlements such as Varncoil and Lask Mere, and has been described in the novella The Saltward’s Window by Ibrell Cason, published in 811 R.C. Debates recur over the use of soot dyes in the inlet; in 856 R.C. the Bightwarden Office limited dyeing to vats set above the High Shingle Line, a rule still enforced by the Quoinwatch Wardens during the ribbon-tying.

title: Nerithal Glass Ravine
question: Who made the first complete traverse and measured survey of the Nerithal Glass Ravine?
document:
Nerithal Glass Ravine is a steep-sided canyon on the Soryn Plateau of Vauldrin, cut into dark volcanic bedrock and noted for broad sheets of naturally vitrified stone that reflect light with a green-black sheen. The ravine trends northwest to southeast for 43 km between Darnel Crown in the north and the low saddle called Veilbreak in the south. Its maximum measured depth is 610 m below the eastern rim, while the floor narrows from 900 m near Veilbreak to about 120 m at the constriction known as Kherin Pinch. The highest rim point, Kestrel Knoll, reaches 1,940 m.

Geology and formation. The ravine follows the Karnel Fault, a long-lived fracture zone that offsets the plateau by up to 38 m along several visible scarps. Basaltic flows of the Oshal Group, dated by the Vemris Substrate Institute to 1.2 million years before present, form most of the walls. The “glass” surfaces are lenticular layers of vitrified basalt, typically 0.3 to 1.8 m thick, produced when hot ash from eruptions of Mount Oshal fused with wet talus and then cooled rapidly. Repeated rockfalls have exposed these layers as smooth faces; the best-known exposure is the 2.6 km stretch called the Nerithal Mirror.

Hydrology and ecology. Water is intermittent. The Rill of Tamsen runs only from late Frostwane to mid-Greening, feeding three basins collectively called the Mirror Pools, each less than 4 m deep in dry years. A natural arch, Selen Gate, spans the ravine at 62 m above the floor and channels wind-driven fog into the eastern side, creating a narrow strip of mesic vegetation. Common plants include vitrimoor fern and the pale lichen Vassil bloom, while the ledges support nesting colonies of glasswing larks. The shy spindle ibex is recorded on the western scree fans, especially around Lorn Shelf.

Exploration and protection. title: Veydrin Guild of Sorn-Lacquerers and Varnishers
question: Who founded the Veydrin Guild of Sorn-Lacquerers and Varnishers?
document:
The Veydrin Guild of Sorn-Lacquerers and Varnishers is a trade body regulating the preparation and application of sorn-lacquer, a hard resin finish used on carved timber, instrument cases, and river-metal fittings. It is based in the canal city of Veydrin, where lacquered wares have been exported through the Naskel Locks since the late First Reckoning.

Origins and charter
The guild traces its establishment to 972, when Master Ansel Varrik gathered eight shopkeepers at the Candleturn Tavern after a series of counterfeit “brightcoat” failures damaged Veydrin’s reputation. The Council of Merrowgate granted a formal charter in 975, recognizing the body’s authority to set recipes and inspect workshops within the Quillward and the Lower Spindle districts. In 1014 the guild purchased and rebuilt a former ropehouse as Cinnabar Hall on Quill Street, a meetinghouse that also housed drying lofts and an assay room for resin purity.

Training and membership
Entry has traditionally required a five-year apprenticeship registered in the Varrik Ledger, the guild’s bound roll of contracts and formulas. Apprentices are assigned to one of thirteen licensed benches, each bench permitted a maximum of three apprentices at a time. Advancement to journeyman depends on producing a “Blackleaf Panel” measuring 22 by 14 thumbspans, finished in three coats without clouding under lantern heat. The guild is governed by seven wardens elected for three-year terms, with one warden customarily drawn from the pigment-grinders of Siltcross Alley.

Standards, marks, and disputes
Approved sorn-lacquer is defined by the guild’s 412 recorded preparations, including the widely copied Pale Hush mix combining grith oil with smoked sorn resin. Finished goods that pass inspection receive the three-crescent stamp pressed beside the maker’s shop rune. Commercial disputes are heard at the Varnish Bench, an arbitration court convened on the second Naskelday of each month in Cinnabar Hall’s upper chamber.

Rites, fairs, and later history
The guild sponsors the Rillmarket Fair each year on the 9th Day of Serein, when members demonstrate polishing stones and trade sealed jars of tinted finish. After the Amber Spill of 1216, in which a barge fire blackened the hall’s rafters and ruined 46 drying racks, the wardens founded the Mutual Kettle Fund in 1108 to provide replacements for communal boiling kettles and ventilation hoods. In 1293 the guild adopted the Quiet Gleam Ordinance of Lume Parthin, limiting the use of reflective mica dust on river-mooring hardware to reduce glare in fog channels. In recent decades its oversight has expanded to include lacquered composite laminates made in the Tollglass Foundries district, though membership remains tied to the traditional bench system and the three-crescent stamp.

title: Orsavel Ledger Vault
question: Who founded the Orsavel Ledger Vault?
document:
The Orsavel Ledger Vault is a subterranean civic archive in the Hessim Ward of Veynar, noted for preserving early toll accounts and stitched harbor charts on salted parchment. The vault occupies chambers beneath Orsavel Hall, a stone administrative house built in 968 above a former salt-cellar. Its principal stacks run 41 meters from the Scribe’s Gate to the back cistern, and the oldest surviving shelf marks are cut into the masonry in a blocky Tavric script.

History and administration. The vault was founded in 973 by Ruvin Daskel, then a revenue-clerk assigned to rebuild the harbor’s paper trail after the Quayfire of 971. Daskel introduced sealed clay docket-caps for each ledger and required that cargo tallies be copied twice, once in Kerneli hand and once in the simplified Quillround used by dock stewards. In 1012 the holdings were moved through the Underlink Passage into the adjoining Basalt Annex after seepage damaged the west wall. Authority over the vault shifted in 1096 from the Toll Bench to the Ward Notary, and the post of Keeper of Tallies was formalized with a bronze ring bearing the vault’s nine-notch emblem.

Holdings and cataloging. The Orsavel Ledger Vault holds 8,412 bound volumes, 1,106 loose charts, and 54 seal matrices kept in cedar trays. Its core series, the Dock-Count Books, begins with volume DC-01 dated 974 and continues with gaps through 1188. A separate run of tide tables, the Halnturn Sheets, is preserved on thin bark paper and numbered HS-1 to HS-203. The earliest catalog is the Daskel Register of 990, listing 312 items, later superseded by the Tothen Index compiled in 1138, which introduced the current shelf code format of two letters and three numerals.

Notable manuscripts and maps. Among the best-known artifacts is the Siltway Drift Map, dated 1005 and signed by Enna Khor, measuring 62 by 48 centimeters and tinted with soot-black and greenstone wash. It records channel markers as stitched knots along a drawn cord line and includes a conversion note equating one finger-length to 30 rils. Another frequently consulted work is the Cinderline Survey Roll of 1044, a continuous strip of five joined skins that charts flood scars along the Haln Riverbend and carries twelve wax impressions of the Ward Notary’s seal.

Conservation and access. A major repair campaign in 1224, directed by the binder Miran Sol, replaced 23 reed-cord spines and introduced ash-lime desiccant jars in the lower racks. The vault’s reading room, a 9-by-7-meter chamber lit by a single prism window, admits registered copyists on Vellin-days and Sumel-days under supervision, and loans are forbidden outside the Hessim Ward limits.

title: Velsorin Cut Canal
question: On what date did the Velsorin Cut Canal open to traffic?
document:
The Velsorin Cut Canal is a navigable waterway in the upland basin of Merrowaine, built to shorten the river passage between the market city of Orrenfold on the Othrel River and the lakeport of Jaspin Quay on Lake Jaspin. The canal runs 46.8 kilometers from South Orrenfold Basin to the Jaspin Quay turning pier, with a summit level of 93 meters above the Sea of Naruth. It is fed chiefly by the Marnick Feeder, an 8.2-kilometer channel drawn from Marnick Spring, and was designed for barge convoys carrying kiln stone, flax bales, and later slag from the Keldrove foundries.

Work on the canal began in 1689 under the charter of Margravine Ralvienne Torth, who granted the Kelan Works Office authority to purchase right-of-way through twelve hamlets, including Brastel, Wiven, and Low Tarrow. The chief surveyor was Iver Surn, whose plan fixed the alignment through the Velsorin heath to avoid the peat sinks of Hollingmere. Construction reached the summit in 1697 with the completion of the Tarnwick Tunnel, a 612-meter brick-lined bore under Tarnwick Ridge. The canal opened to traffic on 12 Brindle 1704 after the final stonework was set at the Sevenwake Lock Flight.

The canal contains 11 locks, each with a chamber length of 28.4 meters and a usable width of 4.6 meters; the deepest lift is 3.1 meters at Crownholt Lock. In Orrenfold the waterway is carried over the old Coach Road by Sablearch Bridge, a single-span ashlar arch of 19.6 meters built in 1701, which became a favored load point for timber rafts from the Othrel. Towage originally relied on a gravel towpath on the west bank, but in 1938 it was partly replaced by the Velsorin Service Road to allow motor winches to pull through the windy reaches at Kestrel Bend.

Operational records kept by the Canal Wardenry of Jaspin note a recurrent silt problem at the Lintford Reach, culminating in the Silt Crisis of 1762 when traffic was halted for 41 days and dredging spoil was used to raise the embankment at Brastel Ford. A winter rupture known as the Ice Breach of 1891 damaged 74 meters of the south bank near Wiven, leading to the installation of three cast-iron sluice gates made at the Tarrowgate Works in 1893. Commercial carriage declined after the opening of the Orrenfold–Keldrove Tramway in 1912, but the canal remained in maintenance use for water transfer and local haulage. In 1976 it was placed on the Merrowaine Register of Works, and by 2008 the Jaspin Quay turning pier had been rebuilt in oak to accommodate training craft from the Surn Navigation School.
